title: Georg Ohm and the Discovery of Ohm's Law (1827)
explainer: In 1827 the German physicist Georg Simon Ohm published a mathematical theory of electricity showing that, for a conductor like a wire or resistor, current is directly proportional to voltage and inversely proportional to resistance — the exact relationship you just used as V = I × R. The law was coolly received in Germany at first and only gained wide acceptance after it was honored abroad, including the Royal Society's Copley Medal in 1841; the ohm, the unit of resistance, was later named for him. It's worth knowing this was an experimentally discovered regularity of real wires and resistors, not a universal definition — which is exactly why it doesn't apply cleanly to a component like an LED, whose forward-voltage drop isn't a fixed resistance.

title: James Prescott Joule and the Law of Electrical Heating (1840s)
explainer: In the early 1840s, the self-taught English scientist James Prescott Joule, experimenting with electric motors in his family's brewery, found that the rate at which a current-carrying conductor produces heat is proportional to the square of the current times its resistance (I²R) — a relationship now called Joule heating. That's the actual physical reason an overloaded wire, a shorted battery, or an undersized resistor gets hot enough to burn skin or melt insulation, which is why checking a resistor's power rating, not just its ohm value, is a real safety habit and not just caution for its own sake. Joule's heating experiments were also an early step toward his later, more famous work pinning down the mechanical equivalent of heat, one of the founding results of thermodynamics.
